#1698. A Thousand Myles

This Monday marks six months since Arsenal defeated Fulham 3-0 at Emirates Stadium. The game offered a rare oasis of calm in an otherwise fraught season of nailbiting wins. The Gunners, in the midst of a five game ‘playoff’ for the league title with Manchester City, as well as a Champions League semi-final against Atletico Madrid on the horizon, raced into a three-goal lead by half-time at the Emirates, earning an uproarious reception as the players made for the tunnel at half-time.

The previous weekend had seen Arsenal labour to a nervy 1-0 win over Newcastle and a stodgy 1-1 away draw with Atletico Madrid. Bukayo Saka had been parachuted back into the team after an extended absence; but it was clear that Mikel Arteta was looking for ways to try to ease the ketchup out of the bottle, so to speak.

Martin Zubimendi, who, at that point had played more league minutes than any other outfield Arsenal player, dropped to the bench. Myles Lewis-Skelly started in midfield for the first time in his short Gunners career. Myles was supposed to start an FA Cup tie at home to Wigan in that position before Riccardo Calafiori was injured in the warm-up, meaning Lewis-Skelly reverted to left-back with Bukayo Saka playing in a central role instead.

The BBC Sport match report for the Fulham game said, ‘Boss Arteta has to be given credit for taking what could be perceived as risk by playing left-back Myles Lewis-Skelly in midfield for the first time and leaving out Martin Zubimendi, who has played the most minutes of any outfielder in the Gunners squad. The 19-year-old Lewis-Skelly looked assured in the role and, with Calafiori, Saka and Eberechi Eze all in the side, the Arsenal attack flowed better than it has done for many weeks.’

Myles kept his place for the second leg of the Champions League semi-final against Atleti and again for the crunch away win at West Ham. He then started the Champions League semi-final. Probably a week prior to that Fulham game, many Arsenal fans were talking of an inevitable summer sale following the purchases of Piero Hincapie at left-back and Martin Zubimendi in midfield.

His homegrown status made him a potentially attractive sale. His path appeared to be blocked. The talk clearly wasn’t lost on Lewis-Skelly. When he posted a picture with the Premier League trophy on his Instagram account, he captioned it ‘pure profit.’ It was an amusing clapback.

His destiny appeared to change with a roll of the dice. Arteta made a brave call to sit Zubimendi down in favour of a teenager who had yet to really play a senior game in central midfield. Lewis-Skelly repaid his manager’s faith. Lewis-Skelly, who had burst onto the scene in an unfamiliar left-back position, had repeated the trick in central midfield.

It is a quite extraordinary achievement for a teenager to break into a team the quality of Arsenal’s twice, in different positions. He has achieved it so matter-of-factly that I feel like everyone has barely noticed. This summer could also have proved complicated for Myles.

Firstly, his late season resurgence wasn’t quite enough to win a place in England’s World Cup squad. I think that was a short-sighted decision from Tuchel. However, in the September international break, MLS started three of England’s four Nations League games in central midfield.

In many ways, being spared an exhausting summer at the World Cup probably did Myles a favour in the long run. It enabled him to play a full pre-season and in central midfield too. With Declan Rice, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi going to the final weekend of the tournament, as well as Odegaard, Eze and Bruno going to the latter stages, he had a clear run at the position.

This put him in a strong position to start the season. However, his pre-season was complicated by two things. The signing of Bruno Guimaraes, who could have offered a further road-block to Myles’ progression. There were also strong rumours that some people in the club (!) were touting Lewis-Skelly around in a bid to raise the funds for a much-needed attacking A-lister.

While this talk was swirling around in the summer, Myles’ response was to score in a pre-season friendly against Como. What followed was even more impressive, Bruno came into the season with some fitness concerns. Lewis-Skelly’s form was such that his presence in midfield made that a total non-issue. He starred in wins at Villa Park and at home to Chelsea.

In truth, I still don’t think Bruno has done enough to firmly dislodge Myles from the role of Declan Rice’s midfield partner. His apprenticeship at left-back has also proved hugely useful and is helping him to pick up even more minutes. At Fleetwood, he played in both positions during the game, while he started games against Everton and Lille at left-back too.

Having a minor and a major is very useful for a young player looking to build his CV. He came on for Bruno in the Allianz last week and, in my view, outshone his more experienced, more expensive teammate. (Please don’t think I am having a dig at Bruno here, he has clearly conjured up some huge contributions this season too).

In a September interview with Men In Blazers, Lewis-Skelly talked about how he uses mindfulness techniques to deal with pressure and nerves. ‘There’s a Buddhism concept; it’s about the monkey mind. It’s practically about the restless mind, how you can jump from concern to concern.

‘So whenever I feel a type of weight, for me it’s important to bring my nervous system down and to bring stillness back to my mind, to be calm. Whether it is through breathing techniques, music or talking with other people, I just feel like it is important I always remain calm.’

It shows in his play and it shows in how he has dealt with certain situations. His re-ascension in the last six months has been very far from frictionless. Nothing has been given, pieces haven’t fallen into place. He has forced his way in and when he got the shirt, he gripped it for all its worth.

Just think how unlikely it felt in January that Lewis-Skelly would be significantly ahead of Zubimendi in the midfield pecking order before the clocks went back for winter. It takes a special player and a special character to negotiate those numerous challenges and to get into this team. He has met those challenges so firmly that we have barely even noticed them. His is a significant talent.

#1697. Arsenal right to appeal Dowman red

Let’s start with the news that Arsenal are set to appeal Max Dowman’s red card against Fleetwood on Tuesday evening. I think that’s probably the right thing to do, because had that gone to a VAR review, I think they’d have really struggled to make a compelling case that this was violent conduct.

Was it a small retaliation? Yes. Did it meet the threshold for violent conduct? Not for me. As laid out in the rules of the game, it is defined thus: Violent conduct is when a player uses or attempts to use excessive force or brutality against an opponent when not challenging for the ball, or against a team-mate, team official, match official, spectator or any other person, regardless of whether contact is made.

So, on that basis I think Arsenal are right to appeal. They might cite other incidents to make their case. Perhaps the fact Cole Palmer received just a yellow card in Chelsea’s last game against Sp*rs for what was a much more violent action against Mateus Fernandes. Imagine if we even used one of our own players, demonstrating how Bruno Guimaraes was allowed to forearm smash Jorginho in the side of the head, but didn’t get sent off because he didn’t use his arm like a weapon (or something).

Mikel Arteta is a man who, just last week, ‘joked’ he had a collection of images to show other managers outside their techincal area 36 times in ten minutes. If you don’t think he can’t dig up a few more examples of players getting away with violent conduct, you haven’t been paying attention. Whether it’s going to be sufficient to have the red card overturned is another thing, but at the very least we should see a reduction in what is, as it stands, a three match ban. I think the red was very, very, very harsh, but to miss three games because of that is absurd and unfair, so I think we’re right to appeal.

Once again though, there’s a conversation to be had about the punishments for red cards, and how it’s kind of ridiculous that every act of violent conduct = a three game ban. Some acts are more violent than others, some really do endanger the safety of an opponent, and yet they’re all treated the same. It’s never made sense to me, and I don’t really understand how there isn’t a disciplinary panel that assesses each sending off and applies the ban after the fact based on the seriousness of the incident.

Despite his frustration in the moment, I’m sure the manager’s view of Dowman’s behaviour might well have softened on watching the replays. In the heat of the moment part of it, I’m sure, is that we currently have Christos Tzolis and Bukayo Saka sidelined while Noni Madueke missed out on the midweek game to protect an ankle knock. So, we’re very light in the wide areas right now, and while the root cause of that might lie more at the door of the Sporting Director, he would have wanted Dowman available this weekend for the trip to Anfield.

I still think Arteta’s reaction was poor, but football is a game of opinions. I’ve seen some suggest if Max is gonna play with the big boys, he’s got to be treated as an equal. Perhaps that’s fair enough, but I’ve never seen Arteta react like that to a senior player being sent off, and we’ve had plenty of red cards during his tenure. You could argue that his age is why it’s different, that we all need to learn lessons when we’re younger in ways that differ from when we’re more grown up.

For me though, as talented as he is and as excited as we are about what he might become, it’s too easy to lose sight of the fact he is just 16, and that does make it different. It was so interesting that last week, after Bukayo Saka got injured against Bayern, there were myriad conversations about how Arteta was culpable to some extent because of how much he asked of the player since his breakthrough. And in the same breath, many of the same people were saying ‘It’s time for Dowman!’. I find it a little hard to square that circle. Do you actually care about the welfare of a young player or not?

I think Arteta has generally been rightly protective of Max. He knows that exposure at this age is something he and his staff have to consider for all kinds of reasons, and his playing time this season has been limited. In this instance though, regardless of the fact it’s just a few sharp words on the sideline, he’s made this a bigger issue than it should have been, with Dowman firmly in the spotlight, and I’ll be curious to see how he addresses it in his pre-Liverpool press conference tomorrow.

#1696. Aberdeen vs Hibernian - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ellis Stevens | 05 Nov 2026 13:54

Aberdeen and Hibernian will meet at Pittodrie Stadium on Saturday evening for a matchday 13 clash in the Scottish Premiership.

The hosts are 10th in the standings with 11 points from 11 games, while the visitors are bottom of the table with eight points from 11 fixtures.

Aberdeen have endured a lacklustre start to the 2026-27 Scottish Premiership campaign, with Stephen Robinson's side sitting 10th in the standings after 11 league games.

The Dons have recorded only three wins and two draws during that time, alongside six defeats, leaving them narrowly just two points above the drop zone and three points above their bottom-placed visitors.

Aberdeen do have a game in hand on the three teams above them, meaning they will have the opportunity to climb up the standings if they secure a victory, while a win on Saturday could also be crucial to avoid slipping into the drop zone.

The Dons will, however, head into the matchday 13 clash short on confidence after suffering three straight defeats, with Scottish Premiership losses to Dundee United (3-2) and Falkirk (1-0) and a heartbreaking late 1-0 loss to Rangers in the Scottish League Cup semi-final last time out.

With their full focus now on improving their league form, the under-pressure Robinson will be desperate for his side to snap their three-game losing streak and claim all three points when they welcome Hibernian to Pittodrie.

Aberdeen have been at their best when playing at their home ground in the league this season, claiming seven of their 11 points from home fixtures, after two wins, one draw and three defeats.

Hibernian, however, have been at their strongest when playing on the road, accumulating seven of their eight points from away matches in the Scottish Premiership.

Aberdeen do not have any injury concerns or absences heading into Saturday's encounter, leaving Robinson with a fully available squad to choose from.

#1695. CM: Dalot could reunite with Amorim at Milan as Man Utd deal winds down

Diogo Dalot has once again been linked with a potential return to AC Milan, where he spent the 2020-21 season on loan.

Calciomercato.com report that Roma’s visit to face Manchester United at Old Trafford will not only be an opportunity for the Giallorossi to face and perhaps erase the ghosts of the past, but also to watch someone up close who could be a name for the not-too-distant future: Diogo Dalot.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The Portuguese full-back’s contract is expiring at the end of next season and although he is happy in Manchester, many clubs are beginning to ask his entourage for details.

Roma were one step away from landing the defender in the summer of 2021 when the Portuguese coach José Mourinho was on the bench. The negotiations dragged on for a long time, but in the end it didn’t go through.

The reason ended up being quite simple: the Red Devils never agreed to a loan with option to buy formula while Roma – who were still severely limited by Financial Fair Play limitations – could not offer anything more.

Dalot knows Italy and Serie A well, and he recently spoke about his loan experience with Milan in an interview with The Player’s Tribune.

“It was one of the most important years of my career. I remember the way the club welcomed me and how welcome I felt in a year that was important to me, one in which I needed to regain my confidence in my football. Milan helped me get back to those levels,” he said.

“Every day, Paolo Maldini was on the sidelines to watch us train. Rain, shine, or cold, he was always there, in a suit and tie. He would say to me: ‘Mark like this’ or ‘Tackle it.’ Other times, he would scold me for trying too hard. ‘You’re an extraordinary player, don’t worry, you’ll see, everything will be fine’.”

As mentioned, Dalot’s deal expires in 2028 but there is the presence of a one-year clause that United can trigger. There are a number of teams monitoring his situation including Inter, Milan and Juventus, who have all enquired in recent weeks.

Nothing concrete has emerged yet, as Dalot happy in Manchester and isn’t thinking about the future. However, if things don’t change, a departure – perhaps even for a low-cost fee – could become a realistic possibility.

With the Rossoneri needing defenders, could they try pounce on a reunion for a versatile player that they and Ruben Amorim know well?

#1694. Chelsea are great entertainers but possess clear weakness

Chelsea are promising to be this season’s Premier League entertainers and yet manager Xabi Alonso seemingly believes less is more when it comes to possession.

Alonso has started with two wins from two league games in charge of Chelsea, with his team scoring seven goals and conceding five. So far, it has been a lot of fun – if not entirely convincing.

But perhaps the most significant numbers are around how much – or how little – Chelsea are having the ball. Having finished their 3-2 victory over Fulham with 38.11 per cent of possession, Chelsea had just 25.6 per cent in the 4-3 success over Brighton and Hove Albion and successfully completed 146 passes. Both were their lowest figures on record in the Premier League.

“The data is not important,” Alonso said. “It’s how you play and what we can do better. I don’t say ‘today we need to have 60 per cent or 20 per cent’. I never talk about those things. It’s about how to prepare, how to be more competitive.”

Chelsea’s third goal against Brighton, scored in the 32nd minute, best summed up the London club under Alonso to date. It took the home side three passes to go from the edge of their own penalty area to João Pedro scoring against his former club.

Jorrel Hato passed the ball to Morgan Rogers, he then released Hato down the left and the wing-back slid the ball across for João Pedro to finish. It was a devastating counter-attack and should have put Chelsea on course for a much easier win.

Joao Pedro finishes off a deadly Chelsea counter-attack and gives the Blues a 3-0 lead 🔥 pic.twitter.com/wAr0ckIgXJ

“After 30 minutes, we are 3-0 and probably, in that moment, we have played too much the result,” Alonso said. “It’s quite normal, it happens in many teams. I am sure in the future we can manage it better.”

It is one thing outscoring Fulham and a depleted Brighton team without having the ball, but can Chelsea do that against the bigger and better teams? We will get an early indicator in the next game against Arsenal at the Emirates.

Alonso’s approach has some similarities to the way in which Antonio Conte set up his Chelsea title-winning team. Just as Conte converted Victor Moses into an effective right wing-back, Alonso started Pedro Neto there on Sunday.

After Roméo Lavia had opened the scoring, it was Neto who grabbed Chelsea’s second goal against Brighton by drifting into the penalty area to finish from Rogers’s low cross.

"It's a nightmare for the goalkeeper!"Bart Verbruggen and Mats Wieffer's collision leads to Romeo Lavia scoring his first goal for Chelsea ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/q5awbdwVV0

"Pedro Neto Pounces!"Morgan Rogers goes past his defender before sliding the ball across to Neto! 💥 pic.twitter.com/WHZCIGsOLl

But whereas Conte’s team gave up little at the back, Alonso’s Chelsea are yet to balance their effective transitional play with shutting out their opponents.

Neto was partly to blame for Brighton’s first goal, as he missed a challenge in the build-up to Malick Yalcouyé’s brilliant volley. Making his Chelsea debut, goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez could do nothing to stop it and can expect to be kept busy this season if things do not change.

“I have come here to challenge and to try and win the Premier League,” Martínez said. “I know the talent we have up front. I try to bring that solidity at the back.”

"Yalcouye with a sumptuous volley!"Malick Yalcouye puts Brighton on the scoreboard with a venomous volley 😳 pic.twitter.com/8UeeyvPjUw

Conte’s Chelsea had N’Golo Kanté to mop up in midfield and that is an area of the pitch that is causing Alonso some difficulties. Manchester City target Enzo Fernández was once again left out of the squad and Moisés Caicedo was not deemed fit enough to start.

Caicedo was eventually thrown on when Chelsea were trying to stop Brighton completing a remarkable comeback, but he was quickly forced off again with an injury. The club have been exploring a move for Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara and that need looks even more pressing now.

“We want the best for the team and that’s why we took a decision [on Fernández] against Luton and today,” Alonso said. “What’s going to develop? We’re not sure. We can prepare. We are preparing for all the scenarios. But I assure you that whatever happens, from Wednesday [when the transfer window is shut] we’ll have a good enough squad to compete in all the Premier League games.”

Chelsea’s new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee had celebrated Lavia’s goal, which came partly as a result of a corner but owed more to a mistake from Brighton goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen.

MacPhee, however, will not have liked Brighton’s second-half goals. It was from a short corner that the visitors managed to work the ball to Pascal Gross and his cross was diverted into his own net by João Pedro.

Joao Pedro puts Pascal Groß's cross into his own net and Brighton have brought it back to 3-2 👀 pic.twitter.com/maBMwVu3DC

Gross’s headed third goal also came at the end of a set-piece, but, fortunately for Chelsea, it was in the sixth minute of added time and Cole Palmer had already made the points safe for the home team before then.

Palmer had done little to impress watching England head coach Thomas Tuchel until he picked up the ball in the 74th minute, shrugged off two Brighton challenges and produced a brilliant finish to beat Verbruggen.

Cole Palmer finishes EXPERTLY to give Chelsea their two-goal cushion back 💥 pic.twitter.com/6xI9W8xe2q

Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton manager, said his team “dominated” the game, but acknowledged: “I think if you spend so much money on these kinds of players, like Rogers, Palmer or João [Pedro], then, of course, a team like Chelsea can rely on this individual quality. And they showed it in certain moments of the game.”

Palmer, João Pedro and Rogers are clearly going to be a huge problem for Chelsea’s opponents. But Alonso’s team cannot rely on having to score three or four goals to win games. And they might need to have a bit more of the ball.

"The game today was a special game for me." João Pedro says he was happy with his performance for Chelsea against Brighton 🔵 pic.twitter.com/fWSqWo7ert

6 - João Pedro today was the sixth player (and first for Chelsea) to score a goal, assist a goal, and score an own goal in the same Premier League game, and first since Tottenham Hotspur's Son Heung-min against Man City in December 2023.Eventful. pic.twitter.com/xRVjqkOY9D

There is no time for Brighton to push for the equaliser as the final whistle is blown at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea make it two wins from two to start the new Premier League season but were pushed all the way by Brighton. It finishes 4-3 at Stamford Bridge.

It could well be the last touch of the game but Brighton have a small amount of hope as Gross heads past Martinez. If that had come a few minutes ago, maybe Brighton could have pushed for a draw.

Brighton have a corner and if they are to have any chance of potentially rescuing a point, they have to score right now. De Cuyper’s inswinger is clipped into a dangerous area but for some odd reason referee Michael Oliver gives Chelsea a free-kick. Absolutely ridiculous decision; there was no foul in any way, shape or form.

Chelsea look to counter through Pedro, who is then brought down by Costinha. It is an easy booking for referee Michael Oliver to give.

How many added minutes will there be? The answer is five minutes.

Boscagli is booked for bringing down Rogers.

This is a concern for Chelsea as Caicedo, who came on as a second-half substitute, is now having to go off injured. In his place is former Brighton man Barco, who slapped Bellingham at the World Cup. Barco is booed vociferously by the travelling Brighton fans.

Meanwhile Leeds are level 1-1 against Brentford at Elland Road thanks to Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser.

Double change for Brighton as Costinha and David replace Wieffer and Kostoulas.

Brighton scored four a week ago against Aston Villa on the opening weekend but have conceded four this weekend. If they can get a goal though soon, it would make the home fans inside Stamford Bridge very nervous.

Kadioglu has an effort from the edge of the Chelsea box but drags his effort wide.

Meanwhile, up in the north east, Isidor has put Sunderland 1-0 up against Fulham at the Stadium of Light.

Palmer has been pretty quiet today but Chelsea’s two-goal lead is restored. He receives it from Pedro and drives forward through the Brighton half. As he approaches the edge of the penalty area, Palmer calmly slots home into the bottom corner.

Cole Palmer finishes EXPERTLY to give Chelsea their two-goal cushion back 💥 pic.twitter.com/6xI9W8xe2q

Tuchel will have like that. He may not have had a brilliant game, but Palmer just scored a brilliant goal. That should be enough for Chelsea.

Fabian Hurzeler turns to his bench for the first time today as Osman comes on for Yalcouye, who was impressive.

Xabi Alonso turns to his bench again as Chavarria replaces Colwill.

We have this news from the Premier League:

#CHEBHAMatch Officials are operating in the second half without communications packs due to an ongoing technical issue. VAR remains in operation via a back-up system using messages sent to the referee's watch and radio communication to the fourth official if required.

Dunk is in trouble. The ball is played forward by Gusto down the right channel to pick out the run of Pedro into the Brighton half. Dunk brings Pedro down but is fortunate that Vuskovic was covering so that is why there is no red card. Dunk is rightly booked.

Chelsea are on the ropes at the moment and Brighton can sense another goal. Boscagli is the latest Brighton player to have an effort and Martinez is forced into a decent save down to his left.

Xabi Alonso is going to respond to the Brighton momentum with a triple change. James, Acheampong and Caicedo replace Neto, Lavia and Fofana.

It is all Brighton and Chelsea are seriously wobbling. Gomez has his fourth chance of the second half and is not far off scoring as his effort hits the side netting. You can sense the anxiety inside Stamford Bridge and it is the travelling Brighton fans making all the noise.

This game is well and truly back on. Chelsea looked in complete control at 3-0 up but now there is just one goal in it. Brighton work a corner short and appear to have wasted the chance but Yalcouye slides a wonderful pass into the right side of the box to pick out the run of Gross, whose shot/cross takes a big deflection off former Brighton man Pedro and goes past Martinez into the Chelsea net.

Joao Pedro puts Pascal Groß's cross into his own net and Brighton have brought it back to 3-2 👀 pic.twitter.com/maBMwVu3DC

Gomez has already missed two chances in this second half and he now has his third opportunity since the break. His powerful effort from the right side of the box forces Martinez into a decent save at his near post...

England head coach Thomas Tuchel is at Stamford Bridge today. He won’t have like Cole Palmer’s miss much and Palmer is probably the only Chelsea attacking player not to have impressed so far. There’s still time, though.

Chelsea have two big chances to score a fourth but cannot take either. First, Neto takes advantage of poor defending from Kadioglu and has a shot saved at the near post by Verbruggen. Then Palmer has a glorious opportunity inside the six-yard box from Rogers’ cross but somehow Palmer guides it over the bar. I am going to say it now that I do not think we have seen an end to the goals today.

Fofana is rightly booked for an earlier challenge on De Cuyper as he completely took him out and Brighton now have a free-kick deep into the Chelsea half after a foul by Neto.

Boscagli clips a lovely free-kick to the back post, where he perfectly picks out Gomez, who has a free header from the edge of the six-yard box but his powerful header goes wide of the far post. That should have been a goal and that is a mighty let-off for Chelsea.

Gomez has a decent chance for Brighton on the edge of the Chelsea penalty area but he fires his effort well wide.

Chelsea attack from back to front, with Martinez launching a long ball forward from inside his own box to pick out the run of Pedro into the Brighton half. Pedro ends up having a shot blocked inside the Brighton penalty area.

Palmer was very influential for Chelsea at Fulham on Monday night and, despite Chelsea scoring three first-half goals, he has been quiet today.

We are back under way at Stamford Bridge. Despite Chelsea being two goals ahead, it does not feel like Brighton are out of this one.

Chelsea 3 Brighton 1Leeds 0 Brentford 1Sunderland 0 Fulham 0

Possession: Chelsea 29%-71% BrightonShots: 9-6Shots on target: 4-3Corners: 2-4Touches in opposition box: 15-10

Chelsea go in 3-1 at half-time, having only had 29.3 per cent of possession. They finished with about 35 per cent possession in the 3-2 victory over Fulham, so it seems Alonso is setting his team up very much as a counter-attacking side. It’s all very Antonio Conte.

Vuskovic has a late effort in the first half from range and it goes just over Martinez’s bar.

The first half is then brought to an end not long after and Chelsea take a 3-1 lead into the break.

The Brighton fans enjoy an audacious Pedro backheel that does not come off. Moments later, Gross clips in a cross from the right that picks out Gomez in the box but his header goes over the bar.

There will be two added minutes at the end of this first half.

There has been a goal in one of the other 2pm kick-offs. At Elland Road, Brentford, who were one of the most impressive teams on the opening weekend, have taken the lead over Leeds through Schade.

After a dreadful clearance from Dunk, Rogers shoots from just outside the box but it goes wide of Verbruggen’s left post.

Pedro has a shot blocked inside the Brighton area before Rogers also has an effort blocked.

At 3-0 down, they looked down and out but maybe the visitors have a route back into the game. Kostoulas is denied by Martinez before the ball comes to Yalcouye, who volleys first time. His emphatic effort smashes off the inside of the far post and into the net. A fine way to score your first Premier League goal and maybe this game is not over quite yet.

"Yalcouye with a sumptuous volley!"Malick Yalcouye puts Brighton on the scoreboard with a venomous volley 😳 pic.twitter.com/8UeeyvPjUw

There have already been three goals in the first half at Stamford Bridge but it is still goalless at Elland Road and the Stadium of Light in the other two 2pm kick-offs.

The Brighton fans have been singing ‘The Falklands are ours’ at Chelsea’s Argentine substitute Valentin Barco. Barco was part of the Argentina squad who celebrated his nation’s World Cup win over England by displaying a Falklands banner. The Brighton fans had also been giving the club’s former striker Joao Pedro some stick. Pedro celebrated his goal right in front of them. Touche.

The Brazilian missed a sitter earlier but he makes no mistake this time and goes to celebrate in front of the travelling Brighton fans. Pedro owes a lot of gratitude from Hato, who drives down Chelsea’s left from inside his own half to the edge of the Brighton box. The Dutchman passes to his left to find Pedro, who takes one touch before clinically slotting home into the far corner. Is that game, set and match?

Joao Pedro finishes off a deadly Chelsea counter-attack and gives the Blues a 3-0 lead 🔥 pic.twitter.com/wAr0ckIgXJ

Brighton have their first real sighter on goal. Gomez clips in a lovely delivery to the far post to pick out the run of Yalcouye into the box. Yalcouye gets to it on the stretch and his effort is straight at Martinez.

Brighton have had 70% possession but their xG currently sits at 0.03. Despite having a lot of the ball, they really have not looked like scoring. You do though have to bear in mind that they are without forwards like Minteh, Rutter and Mitoma due to injury. Will Minteh still be a Brighton player when the window shuts?

How has Pedro missed? The former Brighton man absolutely should have put Chelsea 3-0 up and that could have been game, set and match. The ball is played in behind down the right channel and Neto outmuscles Kadioglu, who goes to ground near the byline. Neto then unselfishly from the right side of the box squares it for Pedro, who takes a few touches before getting his shot away. It seems harder to miss than to score but somehow puts his effort wide of the far post.

After Martinez easily catches a corner from Gross, the Chelsea fans start singing the name of their new goalkeeper.

Brighton are dominating posession but are yet to have a shot. Chelsea meanwhile have had three shots, all on target, and have scored twice.

The hosts have their second inside the opening quarter of an hour. Rogers does well on the left side of the box to hold off Vuskovic before squaring the ball. Neto runs across Kadioglu’s blindside and pokes home first time from eight yards out. Kadioglu should really have dealt with that and was too flat-footed. He should not have allowed Neto to get to that ball first.

"Pedro Neto Pounces!"Morgan Rogers goes past his defender before sliding the ball across to Neto! 💥 pic.twitter.com/WHZCIGsOLl

The travelling Brighton fans are making sure that Pedro knows what they think of their former player.

Up in the stands, England boss Thomas Tuchel is sat next to Brazil manager Carlo Ancelotti, both former Chelsea bosses.

Since the start of the 2024/25 season, no goalkeeper in the Premier League has made more errors leading to goals than Verbruggen’s 10. Second on that list; Sanchez, who is not in the Chelsea squad today.

Brighton win their first corner of the afternoon and Martinez is forced into action, punching away at his near post as the delivery threatened to creep in.

That is an absolute gift for the home side after a huge error from Brighton. Pedro flicks on at the near post and Wieffer makes the block near his own line. Verbruggen then tries to catch the loose ball but he and Wieffer end up getting into each others’ way. The ball then falls to Lavia, who pokes home. As they did at Craven Cottage the other night, Chelsea hit the front early.

"It's a nightmare for the goalkeeper!"Bart Verbruggen and Mats Wieffer's collision leads to Romeo Lavia scoring his first goal for Chelsea ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/q5awbdwVV0

There was a fist pump from Chelsea’s new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee after Romeo Lavia’s goal from the corner. It looks like MacPhee will be claiming credit for that one, even though it came thanks to an error from Brighton goalkeeper Bart Verbruggen. Xabi Alonso also celebrated with MacPhee.

Chelsea win the first corner of the afternoon after Dunk blocked Neto’s cross...

He might be trying to sell his shares in Chelsea, but co-owner Todd Boehly is at today’s game in the Stamford Bridge stands.

Before we get going, Stamford Bridge pays tribute to Bobby Tambling and Ken Bates, who both died over the summer. Wreaths are laid in their memory with their families carrying framed pictures of the two men.

Emiliano Martínez turns 34 on September 2 and by most tangible metrics, the goalkeeper is past his peak.

But it is the intangibles that set Martínez apart and why his availability at a knock-down price from Aston Villa convinced Chelsea to seize a market opportunity.

At £7.5m, Martínez could prove to be Chelsea’s smartest piece of business of the summer and there is little doubt he will be box-office at Stamford Bridge.

Xabi Alonso takes charge of his first home Premier League game in charge of Chelsea as they host Brighton at Stamford Bridge. Both sides were in action in two different competitions on Thursday night. Chelsea reached the League Cup third round as they beat Luton 2-0 at Stamford Bridge, with former Brighton man Danny Welbeck scoring on his debut. Brighton meanwhile confirmed their place in the Conference League group stages with a 4-0 aggregate win over Tromso.

Chelsea began their Premier League campaign last Monday in a west London derby against Fulham at Craven Cottage, winning 3-2 in Alonso’s first game as Chelsea boss. Enzo Fernandez was not involved in Chelsea’s squad against Luton on Thursday and has been heavily linked with a move to Manchester City. Alonso was asked about Enzo’s absence on Thursday and did not confirm whether the Argentine would be involved today.

“It was just because of the game today [on Thursday] and we have other players who need minutes,” Alonso said. “[On Wednesday], in the afternoon. It is a decision that I took. Enzo is a good professional. He is training well and I have nothing to say about this. It was just decisions that we have to take thinking about the game that we were playing tonight [Thursday]. We will see for Sunday [today].”

Brighton began their Premier League campaign in emphatic style as they thrashed Aston Villa 4-0 at home seven days ago. Jack Hinshelwood scored twice in that game but will now miss a number of weeks with an ankle injury. They are also without Yankuba Minteh, who has been linked with a move to Liverpool this summer but is unavailable due to injury.

“When the window is closed I demand from him [Minteh] that he is fully committed to this club,” Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler said. “There are dreams and wishes for players, but in the end we always need to figure out what is best for the club.

“We have had an exchange with him. At the moment he is definitely a Brighton player. It is very important to understand his thoughts but also our planning. As a club we try to develop players. The last few years have shown that the whole environment gave him a lot of trust and belief that he is capable of having this progress. It is always a give and take and he has gotten a lot from us.”

Brighton won both Premier League meetings last season, winning 3-1 in this fixture last September. Brighton have won five of their last eight top-flight meetings with Chelsea. Team news from Stamford Bridge to follow shortly.

Jack Grealish missed Everton's Premier League win over Newcastle on Monday night

#1691. Accrington Stanley vs Wycombe Wanderers - prediction, team news, lineups

By Calum Burrowes | 05 Nov 2026 14:11, Last updated: 05 Nov 2026 20:21

Both looking to reach the second round of the FA Cup once again, League Two side Accrington Stanley welcome third-tier opponents Wycombe Wanderers to the Crown Ground on Saturday afternoon, with both clubs entering the competition at this stage.

The Reds are enjoying their best spell of the season and head into the weekend's clash on the back of a 10-game unbeaten run, while the Chairboys continued their push towards the playoff places last week with a 2-0 victory over Burton Albion.

Accrington Stanley would need to win three matches in this season's FA Cup to equal their best run in the competition, having most recently reached the fourth round during the 2022-23 campaign before being denied another opportunity to repeat that achievement in 2025 when a trip to Anfield ended in a 4-0 defeat.

John Doolan remains in charge of the Reds and will oversee his 135th match as Accrington boss on Saturday, with his side currently enjoying one of the most encouraging spells of his tenure.

The Reds endured a difficult start to the campaign, recording just one victory in their opening eight matches across all competitions, but they have since turned their fortunes around and remain unbeaten since early September.

Impressive victories over top-half opponents such as Cheltenham Town and Gillingham have helped Doolan's side climb to ninth in the League Two table and extend their unbeaten run to 10 matches across league and EFL Trophy action, although seven of those fixtures have ended level after 90 minutes.

Two of those draws came in cup competitions and were ultimately settled by penalty shootouts, but Accrington have still drawn half of their league matches this season, with no side in the English Football League recording more.

Wycombe Wanderers, meanwhile, make the 200-mile-plus journey from Buckinghamshire to Lancashire hoping to extend their unbeaten run to five matches after enjoying an encouraging start under their new manager.

Michael Duff was relieved of his duties at the beginning of September and replaced by Tom Hounsell, who initially took charge on an interim basis before being handed the job permanently following an impressive start.

Since his arrival, the Chairboys have suffered just one defeat in 10 matches across all competitions, losing 4-1 to Luton Town, while their improved results have lifted them from the relegation zone to 13th in the League One table, leaving them four points adrift of the top six.

Their most recent victory came last weekend, when goals from Jayden Wareham and Cauley Woodrow secured a comfortable 2-0 win over Burton Albion.

Hounsell has overseen a 60% win rate since taking charge, marking an impressive beginning to his time at Adams Park, and he will now prepare for his first FA Cup fixture as Wycombe look to reach the second round for the fourth consecutive season.

Wycombe Wanderers form (all competitions):

Louie Moulden is expected to retain his place between the posts, with Devon Matthews, Farrend Rawson and Joseph Anderson likely to continue as part of a familiar back three.

As for the visiting Chairboys, Hounsell could take the opportunity to rotate his squad and rest a few key players with a demanding run of fixtures awaiting his side over the coming weeks.

Former England and Liverpool striker Danny Ings has largely been used from the bench since joining Wycombe but could be handed a starting opportunity in the FA Cup this weekend.

#1690. Dowman ban upheld, football’s rules need to change

Let’s start again with Max Dowman whose three match ban was upheld after Arsenal’s appeal against the red card failed. The club had made the bid on the basis of wrongful dismissal and excessive punishment, but the claim was dismissed by an independent regulatory commission who will publish their ‘written reasons’ in due course. Thanks for that.

You will already know I think this is too severe. I thought the sending off was harsh, especially with the video evidence that backed the appeal, and for a player to miss three games for what was such a minor reaction to a heavy challenge is really unfair. And I would say that if this were an Arsenal player or not. It’s another example of how we hear about the concept of player protection all the time, but the reality is there have been countless incidents which could have been used to demonstrate there’s a seriousness about that but it never, ever happens.

How absurd is it that Max Dowman will serve the same ban as Ryan Shawcross got for snapping Aaron Ramsey’s leg in two? Remember when Dan Smith launched himself at Abou Diaby’s ankle, putting him out of the game for 9 months and causing an injury so severe it plagued the rest of the Frenchman’s career? He didn’t even get a red card that day, so the next time you see Dermot Gallagher pontificating on Sky about how a referee got an obviously wrong decision right, apply that context (he was the ref at the Stadium of Light that day).

Football has a problem with actual violent conduct, but chooses to deal with it by trying to make us think performative infractions like Dowman’s are worthy of the same punishment as the acts of real violence. The dangerous tackles, the two-footed leaps (which seem to creeping back into the game a bit, probably because they’re not being punished), pushing an opposition player when they’re in the air, these things are not on the same scale. If what Dowman did is worthy of a three game ban, the next time someone goes studs first over the ball into the shins of their opponent, they should get ten games at least.

But we know that’s not going to happen. Almost as long as this blog has been going (coming up on 25 years now!), I’ve made the case for there to be a sliding scale of punishment for acts that meet the definition of violent conduct. Some things are just more violent than others, but as long as this blanket punishment of three games regardless of the seriousness of the incident is in place, the more those in charge do the game and the players a disservice.

Still, it is what it is now, and Arsenal will have to live without Dowman for the games against Liverpool, Hull City, and the away trip to Newcastle on the far side of the upcoming November Interlull. He could well have been involved at some point this weekend against Liverpool, but now we’re sweating on the fitness of Noni Madueke, with Eberechi Eze the only other option for the left hand side. There are some whispers that Christos Tzolis could be back in contention for Sunday, which would be a very welcome boost, but the forward line looks a bit light for a game of this significance.

Tuesday’s game against Fleetwood will live in the memory because of the giant killing aspect, but for two young Academy players, it’s a night that will hopefully be formative. For Dowman, whether you think what he did was worthy of a red card or not, there’s a lesson to learn about how you react. To be quite honest, I think there’s something to like about the way he was prepared to stick up for himself against a grown man who wanted to ‘leave a bit on him’, as they say. The talented players are the ones who get kicked most though, and it’s something he’s going to have to contend with as his career develops. Just ask Bukayo Saka. The two have plenty of time on their hands right now, and I’m sure it will be part of his footballing education.

The other player is Marli Salmon who probably should have done better on their goal, but for me is less culpable overall than some of the senior players who didn’t perform at the right level. Arsene Wenger once said:

You pay for the education of young players with points. If I play a 20-year old centre back, I know he’ll cost me points during the season and I have to stand up for that. A less talented 28 year old would cost me less points. However, by 23/24 you have a player.

Marli Salmon is 17. He didn’t cost us any points. There’s a long way still go in his development, but I’m sure with the coaching staff they’ll go over what happened against Fleetwood and he will learn from it. It is more difficult for young defenders than young attackers too. A mistake at the top end of the pitch, like Dowman scuffing a shot wide from a position he probably ought to score from, doesn’t feel quite as costly as a forward running off a young defender to score the opening goal of the game. But again, it’s all part of the process, every young player makes mistakes, it’s how you then use them to improve that counts, and I’m sure he’ll do that.

Right, let’s leave it there for now. The Arsecast is below if you haven’t had a chance to listen yet, and a bit later on we’ll have a preview podcast for you over on Patreon once we’ve heard what Mikel Arteta has had to say at his press conference. Also, our Patreon members get the first chance to order our upcoming limited edition book The 22, that’s happening at 3pm today. If you fancy coming to the launch in London next Friday, there are still some spots left but you have to register here – https://www.eventbrite.co.uk/e/the-22-the-launch-tickets-2003029364750

Camarda was present at the Paolo and Larissa Pini Institute for a one-on-one discussion with students and a lesson with the Sport and Health tutors, to help promote the value of sport and the desire to continue practicing it.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It was the player who asked the students questions for the most part, not the other way around. Camarda questioned them on their motivations behind playing sports, if they have ever considered quitting and if so why they chose to continue.

Camarda himself is having to be patient and to wait for opportunities at the moment given his lack of playing time under Ruben Amorim, which may even mean evaluating another loan move away from his boyhood club.

#1688. Arteta didn’t see the reaction to the reaction but reacts to the reaction to the reaction

Morning all, let’s do a bit of a Saturday round-up ahead of tomorrow’s game against Liverpool which we’ll cover in more detail then.

First, Mikel Arteta responded to the appeal against Max Dowman’s red card, and said:

We’re very disappointed, to be fair, especially with the reckless tackles that he receives – his reaction is minimal in relation to the action. We’re disappointed it hasn’t been overturned having watched it back.

We’ve put every argument on the table to make a case for it – not only the action that is so evident, but when you look back in slow motion, the previous action and Max’s action is clear. Obviously, we have a very different opinion. I think you also have to look at the context of the player, the age and what happened previously.

You already know what I think. Ultimately, there’s only one person who was in any danger of being hurt on that pitch on Tuesday evening, and it was Dowman himself. Arteta said:

It could have been really bad, and we’re lucky today that he hasn’t had a broken foot – that’s clear.

But as we’ve discussed this week, football’s attitudes to things like minor retaliation versus a ‘crunching’ tackle are a bit topsy-turvey, and Dowman is a victim of that. The fact they didn’t even reduce the ban, which there is definitely precedent for, suggests to me they have chosen to overlook what the replays show, and that’s quite disappointing.

Still, it was interesting to hear Arteta reference Dowman’s age when referring to this, then a bit later on suggesting that if he’s going to play with the big boys, he’s not going to get any special treatment because of how young he is. There’s been discussion and debate about the manager giving the 16 year old a bit of an earful on the sideline as he went off, but in this instance he stood behind his ‘tough love’ approach. Referencing the fact Dowman had been sent off for England U19s a few weeks ago for something similar, and the conversation they’d had in the dressing room before they went out, he said:

I haven’t seen the reaction to my reaction, whether it’s positive or negative. But you need to understand the context, the relationship that I have with him and what we discussed just before we went out.

You want to see the reaction of his teammates? When they have to play with 10, you want to see that? This is the environment and this is the reality. Otherwise we are in Disneyland, we are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League at this level and we look after him so much that you cannot imagine. But at the same time we are going to demand of him, like to anybody else, because he needs to earn the right to play. Otherwise the rest of the boys, what are they going to tell me? You need to be fair.

As I said yesterday, hopefully it’s a learning moment for Max, one he can carry forward for when he returns and beyond. Professional football is absolutely ruthless, there will be managers/players who will try and expose that youthful temperament again, and we know how they’ll do it. He’ll get kicked again, they’ll try and bully him again, but next time he’s got to remember that referees are more inclined to punish the guy who retaliates than the one who perpetrates the first offence. It’s upside down, of course, but that’s the environment in which we exist and one he’s got to get to grips with. I suspect that whatever your own view of Arteta’s reaction, that message will have been made loud and clear to Max Dowman this week.

Elsewhere, because this is very, very funny, Aston Villa say they’re going to take legal action against Jamie Carragher for some comments he made on a podcast. Via their official social media channels, they released a statement which said:

Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the club and its fans. Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, chairman.

Apparently Carragher’s remarks were about Unai Emery potentially joining Man Utd, and pointing out that there is a kind of pecking order in terms of club stature. Which, regardless of the fact United are a mess right now, is unquestionably true in terms of the size of the fanbase, the history etc. Villa are a successful club with good history of their own, but United are – in this general context – a bigger club. Like Barcelona are bigger than Valencia, like Bayern Munich are bigger than Borussia Dortmund, like some side from the Isle of Man third division are bigger than Sp*rs.

How thin skinned and pathetic do the people running Villa have to be to take exception to something Carragher said, to then ruminate on it, decide that legal action is the best course of action, and then make it public? Genuinely it’s hilarious and embarrassing. Also, I’d be quite happy for Emery to take over at United. He’s done a fantastic job at Villa, but as Arsenal fans we know he’s exactly the man you need to take over a club that’s something of a sleeping giant and a mess on and off the pitch. Emery in at Old Trafford all the way, in my opinion. They’d be facing that side from the Isle of Man third division in no time.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. Happy Halloween, I hope your little visitors aren’t too scary later on, and that your dogs don’t freak out with the fireworks too much.

#1686. Forward line must step up to help deliver first Anfield win in 14 years

After a midweek journey to the north-west for the EFL Cup, we’re back in that neck of the woods today to face Liverpool in the Premier League.

The team news from the press conference was relatively promising, with Declan Rice, Riccardo Calafiori and Christos Tzolis all in training ahead of the game, and Mikel Arteta sounded relatively positive on Noni Madueke who missed out on the trip to Fleetwood Town. With Bukayo Saka out, and Max Dowman obviously suspended, he’ll start on the right and hopefully this run in the team will see him deliver a little more in terms of end product.

He got the backing of the manager beforehand, who said of him reaching his potential:

He has all the potential to do it, he has all the attributes to do it. He certainly has the will to do it because when you see him train every single day, he’s one of the players who enjoys the practice the most and wants to expose himself to all kinds of situations and actions. Now he needs to put the performance on the pitch.

Eberechi Eze should start on the other side, looking for his first Premier League goal contribution of the season, and I think the only other decision to be made is the construction of the midfield. Will it be Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes with Rice and Martin Odegaard? My own preference for a tricky away game is probably for Myles, because if you need to change something the Brazilian has attributes you can count on for that. However, he started him away in Munich, brought Lewis-Skelly on in his place when we were 2-1 down and that turned out all right. So, let’s see.

My guess is we’ll see: Raya, Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori, Rice, Guimaraes, Odegaard, Eze, Madueke, Havertz

After two goals in the first three games of the season, Kai Havertz has gone five without a goal in the Premier League, so today would be a good day for him to get back on track and to find some form again. I’d like to see him stay more central, to be something of a focal point rather than drift around the way he likes to. Perhaps when you face good centre-halves as he will today that’s part of how you disrupt them, but right now there’s real focus on our strikers and what they’re delivering (or not delivering as the case might be), and I hope that he, and Viktor Gyokeres when he gets a run later in the game, can produce what we need.

As for today’s opposition they’re still a bit of a work in progress under Andoni Iraola, but they seem to be getting to grips with what he wants. It took him a bit of time at Bournemouth, and the same seems to be true at Anfield, but Liverpool’s only defeat of the season was to Man City, collapsing late on after going down to 10 men. They have a couple of injuries, but in Alexander Isak they have a dangerous centre-forward in good form, and a player who has caused our central defenders plenty of problems in the past. Gabriel and Konsa will have to be at their best today, the sharpness of his movement in the box is really tricky to deal with.

It’s been 14 years since we last won away at Liverpool in the league, something Arteta views as a record to change:

It’s an opportunity. I came here and in many places we were 20, 22 years, 18 years without winning, and we’ve been doing all these things, so on Sunday, that’s the opportunity that we have.

Regardless of how you might feel about going out of the League Cup, you can be sure Mikel Arteta’s pride will have been hurt by both the defeat and the gleeful reaction to it in certain quarters. He will demand a response from his team today, and if that brings about a win at a ground that hasn’t been favourable for us in recent years, then you wouldn’t be at all surprised. Nevertheless, I think today will be a real test for two sides, neither of whom are in tip-top form right now, and two excellent coaches whose connection and friendship goes back years to add an extra dimension to proceedings.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. Another victory for the Tangerines on Saturday could lift them fourth in the standings and only a point behind third-placed Hearts, while they also have a game in hand on several teams below them after last weekend's match was postponed due to Hearts' involvement in the Scottish League Cup.

Motherwell, meanwhile, have had three days fewer rest than their hosts after taking on St Mirren at the weekend, although they will be rejuvenated after securing a much-needed 1-0 win in that clash, marking the end of a disastrous seven-game winless run.

The Steelmen, who actually started the Scottish Premiership season with two wins and two draws from their first four, endured a catastrophic six-game losing run from early September to early October, which was eventually ended with a 2-2 draw against St Johnstone.

Following their much-needed 1-0 triumph at the weekend, Motherwell are now unbeaten in their last two and have climbed to ninth in the table, although they still hold just a three-point lead over 11th-placed Kilmarnock.

Alfred Johansson, who faced a lot of pressure and scrutiny during their miserable winless run, will be eager for his side to record another positive result on Saturday, further easing the pressure on his role as well as extending their lead over the drop zone.

Motherwell must improve defensively if they are to secure a result against Dundee United, as only Kilmarnock (28) have conceded more than their 20 goals conceded this season.

The Steelmen will also be hoping to improve upon their underwhelming record on the road, having won one, drawn two and lost three of their six away fixtures in the Scottish Premiership this season, scoring 10 and conceding 12 goals in that time.

Motherwell will draw confidence from their recent record against Dundee United, as despite failing to win either of their last two visits to Tannadice Park, the Steelmen are unbeaten in their last four meetings with the Tangerines, including a 3-0 win at the beginning of this season.

Dundee United will be unable to call upon Will Ferry, Emmanuel Agyei and Mehdi Merghem due to injury issues, while Neil Farrugia is also unavailable after suffering a muscle injury in the draw with Celtic.

Farrugia could be replaced by Daniel Bennie in attack, while the remainder of the team that started the draw against the reigning champions on October 28 are likely to feature in this one.

Motherwell are contending with ongoing injury issues to Dylan Williams and Paul McGinn, while the remainder of the squad is available for selection.

Following the 1-0 win against St Mirren in their last match, Johansson could opt to name an unchanged team on Saturday, including goalscorer Lukas Fadinger alongside Joe Hodge in the middle of the park.

#1682. Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal: Resolute Gunners dig in for a big Anfield win

Fourteen years is a long time to wait for a win at any stadium, but Arsenal ensured all three points returned from Anfield to North London for the first time since 2012 yesterday.

The surprise in the team line-up was the return of Christos Tzolis who had missed a month, more or less, with a hamstring injury. If it initially felt a bit harsh on Eberechi Eze, Mikel Arteta’s post-game comments about him barely making the game because of an injury problem of his own made it make more sense.

Early on, we were really good. Plenty of the ball, playing it well in their half, and lots of control. Liverpool looked a bit off the pace, and in the opening minutes young midfielder Trey Nyoni was lucky to escape without some sanction for a nasty foul on Martin Odegaard. I think it was much more mistimed than malicious, but studs down the Achilles is never good, and we saw Crystal Palace striker Jean Philippe Mateta see red for something similar on Saturday evening.

The early pressure paid dividends when Liverpool were a little sloppy at the back. Odegaard pounced to recover the ball, it was fed to Noni Madueke via Bruno Guimaraes, and when Declan Rice overlapped, his precision ball to the back post found Kai Havertz for a tap-in to make it 1-0. That makes it 5 assists so far this season for the midfielder, all of them from open play as well, and his presence in this team reminds me so much of Patrick Vieira. Not that they’re the same kind of player, but that his importance and stature is just fundamental to us. The desire he showed with that overlap is, essentially, what cracked this game open in our favour.

There was another back post chance for Havertz, almost getting on the end of a deflected Guimaraes shot, but after that – as happens so often at Anfield – the momentum changed. This time there was no Granit Xhaka style confrontation to act as a catalyst, the game just shifted and in the final 20 minutes of the first half we rode our luck a bit.

Liverpool started to play around our box and deliver dangerous balls. One almost found Alexander Isak but a combination of David Raya and Ezri Konsa was enough to see it trickle wide. Florian Wirtz hit the bar with a free kick, and Liverpool wanted a penalty when Tzolis looked to pull back Cody Gakpo but I don’t think there was enough in that one. The next one, however, oooof.

Liverpool put in another dangerous cross, Isak was there to head towards goal from close range, and Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull absolutely prevented him from making contact with the ball. You know my rule of thumb with penalties: how would I feel it were given, or not given, up the other end, and if we didn’t get that I’d be fuming. It’s a penalty all day long, and even if the ref didn’t quite see the foul well enough, the VAR officials really ought to have suggested an on-field review. I found the focus on Isak’s reaction a bit odd. Surely the onus is on the officials to recognise what we’ve all seen without a player having to prompt them in that direction, but we got so, so lucky there.

As we did when Alexis Mac Allister ran into the box and, unmarked from 10 yards out, headed the ball over the bar when he absolutely should score. That was a very bad miss from a Liverpool perspective, and a huge chance to equalise just before the break. We needed half-time, and despite the fact Liverpool enjoyed plenty of the ball in the early part of the second period, they looked a lot less dangerous.

My explanation for this is that we leaned into one of our great strengths, which is our defensive organisation and discipline. I thought Konsa was outstanding, but so too was Riccardo Calafiori at left-back whose one on one defending has improved massively. He dealt with Gakpo, he then had to contend with Rio Ngumoha, and I just loved the concentration as he focused on the ball and more often than not prevented Liverpool from creating danger.

Myles Lewis-Skelly came on midfield, Odegaard’s pressing was relentless, and as I remarked on BlueSky afterwards, if this team could attack half as well as it can defend, we’d be the best team in the world by a mile. There were moments when we could have countered better and with more pace, but we still found some threat in the second 45. The best chance fell to Tzolis, set up by Madueke, and his first-time shot was heading for the bottom corner but for a brilliant save from Alisson.

Liverpool threw the kitchen sink at it from the bench, but it made little difference. Mac Allister then got a bit naughty, slapping Odegaard on the back of the head, then collapsing to the ground to make it look as if Madueke had leaned his head into him. Replays showed that didn’t happen, and it was pretty pathetic from the Argentina international. I guess, as well as being a risible piece of play-acting, there was an element of desperation to it, because Liverpool huffed and puffed but could not blow our house down because of how defensively outstanding we are as a team.

For the first time in Premier League history, Liverpool finished a home game without a shot on target, which tells you something. It probably tells you just how much that Timber shirt pull had an impact because a striker like Isak would at least have tested David Raya from there, but more broadly it tells you that this is a team who look laser-focused on their target this season which is to retain the title – something we’ve never done in the modern era.

Afterwards, I thought the manager’s turn of phrase was interesting when he referred to it as ‘a mission’, saying:

Just loving the mission and the mission was something that we didn’t accomplish in 14 years. You really need to enjoy that. If you don’t, there will be a moment that you will switch off and they will punish you. I think the way we competed and played and the chances that we generated as well, it was really impressive so I’m really happy.

He’s obviously referencing winning away at Liverpool for the first time in such a long time, but I think it applies to the season as well. And, as I referenced in yesterday’s blog, there was a response to the midweek defeat to Fleetwood Town. If that was a result that as fans we could find relatively easy to compartmentalise, I don’t think the same is true for this manager because we know he wants to win every game, and it how much it stings when we don’t – especially against lower league opposition. He expected his side to deliver, saying:

It was a feeling, how the hell can that happen? How can you get out of the cup when you shoot 27 times? We had the chances that we had against a team that had put one shot on target and then you look so silly. Then you have to go to Anfield and say, how can I lift those players up? I had a feeling and I said, now is the moment. We’re going to have to dig deep, have an element of luck at times and for sure a lot of quality in the key moments and we’ve done it.

Which I think is a pretty fair assessment. We did a lot of stuff very well, we had moments of luck – which you so often need in a game like this to take all three points – but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusions that this was anything other than the champions demonstrating our title credentials again. In every season, regardless of how good you are, you need the rub of the green from time to time, like a Ruud van Nistelrooy penalty miss at Old Trafford, or Mateus Fernandes missing a huge chance for West Ham. It doesn’t change the inherent quality you possess or what you’re capable of doing, and in the cold light of day it should make you more driven to ensure you widen the margins – and by that I mean delivering a bit more in the opposition’s final third.

However, no complaints this morning. We had a job to do, and a difficult one at that, and we did exactly that to put us back on top of the table. It’s a nice place to be, but it’s still so early in the season I think we should dismiss any chat about what it means at this point. We can be impressed, but still cognisant of the fact there’s still a long, long way to go.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now, but we will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on today. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around noon or so. Until then, have a good one.

#1681. Arsecast Extra Episode 719 – 02.11.2026

Welcome to another Arsecast Extra, the Arsenal podcast, with myself and James from @gunnerblog.

In this episode we look back at the massive win at Anfield on Sunday after Kai Havertz’s first half goal was enough for all three points. We analyse the Gunners strong start to the game, and opportunities to score a second, before the game swung back towards the home side in the last part of the first half. There’s discussion of Jurrien Timber’s foul on Alexander Isak which probably should have seen Liverpool awarded a penalty, and the big miss from Alexis Mac Allister, before we look at how Arsenal’s hugely impressive defensive strength kept the opposition at arm’s length for the second half, and what this result means for the title challenge even at this relatively early point of the season. In part two we answer questions about egregious play-acting, Mikel Arteta’s subs, Declan Rice’s standing in the pantheon of Arsenal signings, Bruno Guimaraes’ integration thus far, and lots more.

#1680. Newcastle look like a team bereft of energy and inspiration under Matthias Jaissle - as Everton continue to thrive without Jack Grealish after another impressive victory, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 17:16 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 18:11 EDT, 2 November 2026

Jack Grealish was pictured enjoying a cracking night out in Newcastle last year. Here, his Everton team-mates had just as good a time, albeit in a far more sober state.

The Manchester City loanee was left at home after last week’s ‘breach of club discipline’. At least, home is where the club hoped he would be.

And, if he was, Grealish would have watched Everton record a deserved win. He might even have raised a toast, so accomplished an away performance was this.

David Moyes had dropped the winger for last Thursday’s 3-1 win over Newcastle in the Carabao Cup after he missed training following another alleged night on the town. And again, without him, they were too good for Matthias Jaissle’s sorry and directionless Newcastle.

It is the Toon Army, rather, in need of a bender right now. They really aren’t very good - no shots on target before injury-time - and it is remarkable to think they would have gone seventh with victory. That position is now occupied by Everton, who were more skilful and more savvy from start to finish and won thanks to Thierno Barry’s goal just after the break. The scoreline was not a reflection of their superiority.

Jaissle said: ‘We were not brave enough to break the line and play on the ground. We saw it in training, but there was almost nothing to see from these aspects in the game.

Everton, who were more skilful and more savvy from start to finish, won thanks to Thierno Barry’s goal just after the break

Jaissle’s promise has been a team who hunt in packs, yet they were hiding en mass here

‘We have a clear identity of how we want to play - to bring the opposition in stressful situations high in the pitch. We spoke about creating one-on-one situations. The plan was not to play the long balls.’

The opening half hour had been a side-show in two managers betraying varying degrees of frustration. Jaissle buried his fist in his palm every time Everton played through his team at will. And Moyes muttered expletives when his side were unable to take advantage. It was clear he sensed this was there to be won. It was less clear how they would achieve that when Barry was swiping at fresh air six yards from goal.

Newcastle (4-2-3-1): Hornicek 4; Dedic 4, Schar 5, Burn 5, Hall 5; Gonzalez 4 (Steur 64, 6), Joelinton 4 (Ramsey 76, 5); Elanga 4 (Murphy 76, 5) Willock 4 (Wissa 64, 5), Barnes 5; Osula 4.

Everton (4-2-3-1): Pickford 6; O’Brien 7, Tarkowski 7, Branthwaite 7, Mykolenko 7; Garner 7, Armstrong 7; Rohl 6, DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 6; Barry 7.

By the 28th minute, the home fans were booing after yet another aimless long ball. Vertical football, Jaissle has called it, getting the ball forward quickly. Yet more boos on the whistle for half-time told you the locals fear they are going backwards. Everton’s Harrison Armstrong, the half’s brightest midfielder, had only just swiped wide from 12 yards when he should have scored, and that would have been deserved.

The Toon Army were soon cheering, when a fella in jeans kicked a ball through a hole to win a trip to Las Vegas. It was the first effort on target by anyone on the field all evening. Newcastle’s first-half woe was summed up by one free-kick, worked short, that was then chipped straight out of play by Amar Dedic. Jaissle shot to his dugout to watch a replay of what had gone wrong - someone should have told him such footage could not be re-shown pre watershed.

The first effort on target brought the first goal in the 49th minute, and it was no surprise when it came Everton’s way. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall played the sort of pass of which Newcastle were seemingly incapable - low, incisive and accurate - and that set Tyrique George away. His shot was not particularly hard, but then Lukas Hornicek’s attempt to save it was not particularly convincing. As the ball squirmed through his grasp, Barry was quickest to follow up for a tap-in. Newcastle appealed offsides against both George and the scorer, but the truth was that Everton’s players were just sharper in every phase. The time afforded to the excellent Dewsbury-Hall to pick that pass was also a scandal.

Jaissle’s promise has been a team who hunt in packs. They were hiding en mass here. The head coach looked to his bench and called for the popular midfielder Sean Steur. The Dutch teenager’s popularity has been enhanced by him not being in the side of late. The cheer for his introduction, as replacement for the leaden-booted Nico Gonzalez, was almost as big as for the sharp-shooter in Levi’s.

Immediately, Steur impacted. From one smart pass to Harvey Barnes the winger crossed and Anthony Elanga almost stole in to score at the far post. The Geordies have been right to call for his involvement in a team so void of inspiration and positive energy.

It was not long, however, before a chorus of ‘attack, attack, attack’ emerged from the Gallowgate End, and that is never a good sign. Substitute Jacob Ramsey was then sent off for a second booking to compound the home misery.

Meanwhile, the fan bound for Vegas was probably checking for the next flight.
